name: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
title: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
answer: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of finding and executing a trade across one or more decentralised exchange pools rather than sending the entire order to a single venue. The goal is to reduce price impact, account for pool fees and gas costs, and capture better net prices for the trader. It covers single-chain and multi-hop paths, where a swap may pass through several token pairs, as well as splitting an order across pools with different liquidity depths and fee tiers. The field sits at the intersection of market microstructure, optimisation and smart contract execution.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of finding and executing a trade across one or more decentralised exchange pools rather than sending the entire order to a single venue. The goal is to reduce price impact, account for pool fees and gas costs, and capture better net prices for the trader. It covers single-chain and multi-hop paths, where a swap may pass through several token pairs, as well as splitting an order across pools with different liquidity depths and fee tiers. The field sits at the intersection of market microstructure, optimisation and smart contract execution.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Routing systems run on blockchain nodes and remote procedure call endpoints that provide current pool reserves, fee parameters and pending transaction state. Off-chain routing engines query these data sources, simulate candidate trades, and then submit one or more transactions to an aggregator contract or directly to the AMMs. The infrastructure includes gas price oracles, token allowance management, and mempool monitoring to detect competing transactions. On Ethereum and compatible networks, the router must also account for block space and transaction ordering.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by modelling each AMM as a mathematical function that maps reserves to price, such as the constant product formula used by many pools. A router enumerates possible paths and split fractions, estimates the output amount and gas cost for each candidate, and selects the combination with the best expected net result. Some systems use linear programming or convex optimisation to allocate order size across pools, while others rely on heuristic search over a graph of token pairs. The calculation is repeated close to execution time because pool reserves change with every block.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risks in routing include exposure to sandwich attacks, front-running and other forms of maximal extractable value, where a third party can reorder transactions to profit at the trader's expense. Smart contract risk, failed transactions from stale quotes, and slippage beyond a set tolerance are operational concerns. Provenance of pool data matters because a router that reads manipulated or outdated reserves can produce poor routes. Governance of AMM parameters, such as fee switches or pool upgrades, also affects routing outcomes, and the area sits within broader regulatory uncertainty around decentralised finance.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Routing is moving toward intent-based execution, where a user states a desired outcome and competing solvers propose and fill the best route. Cross-chain routing and unified liquidity across layer 2 networks are active areas of development. Dynamic fee mechanisms and more granular pool data are likely to make routing more responsive to short-term volatility. Machine learning may be used to forecast gas prices, liquidity changes and adversarial behaviour, but the core routing problem remains constrained by on-chain state and execution cost.
